claim: All organisms on Earth are exposed to low doses of natural radioactivity.
source: All organisms on Earth are exposed to low doses of natural radioactivity but some habitats are more radioactive than others.
evidence: This is a general statement about natural radioactivity exposure that draws from established scientific knowledge about Earth's environment.

claim: Some habitats are more radioactive than others.
source: All organisms on Earth are exposed to low doses of natural radioactivity but some habitats are more radioactive than others.
evidence: This is a general statement about variation in natural radioactivity that is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The mitochondrial mutation rate increased on average by 60% when radioactivity increased by a factor of three in waterlouse species.
source: We found that the mitochondrial and nuclear mutation rates across a waterlouse species' genome increased on average by 60% and 30%, respectively, when radioactivity increased by a factor of three.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis presented in the study.

claim: The nuclear mutation rate increased on average by 30% when radioactivity increased by a factor of three in waterlouse species.
source: We found that the mitochondrial and nuclear mutation rates across a waterlouse species' genome increased on average by 60% and 30%, respectively, when radioactivity increased by a factor of three.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis presented in the study.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the level of radioactivity and the probability of G to T (and complementary C to A) mutations.
source: We also found a positive correlation between the level of radioactivity and the probability of G to T (and complementary C to A) mutations, a hallmark of oxidative stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational spectrum analysis presented in the study.

claim: G to T (and complementary C to A) mutations are a hallmark of oxidative stress.
source: We also found a positive correlation between the level of radioactivity and the probability of G to T (and complementary C to A) mutations, a hallmark of oxidative stress.
evidence: This is supported by references to established scientific literature on oxidative stress and mutation patterns.

claim: Low doses of natural bedrock radioactivity influence the mutation rate possibly through the accumulation of oxidative damage, in particular in the mitochondrial genome.
source: We conclude that even low doses of natural bedrock radioactivity influence the mutation rate possibly through the accumulation of oxidative damage, in particular in the mitochondrial genome.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data presented in the study and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Natural radioactivity is the main natural source of exposure to ionizing radiations on Earth.
source: Natural radioactivity is the main natural source of exposure to ionizing radiations on Earth.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about radiation sources.

claim: Natural radioactivity is generated by cosmic radiation or by radionuclides released from the bedrock.
source: Natural radioactivity is generated by cosmic radiation or by radionuclides released from the bedrock.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about sources of natural radioactivity.

claim: Bedrock radioactivity remained mainly stable until 2 billion years ago, when it began to slowly decrease.
source: While levels of cosmic radiation fluctuates over time due to cosmic events such as supernovae or solar flares, bedrock radioactivity remained mainly stable until 2 billion years ago, when it began to slowly decrease (Karam and Leslie, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Karam and Leslie, 2005.

claim: Bedrock radioactivity depends on the nature of the rocks which extensively varies spatially.
source: Bedrock radioactivity depends on the nature of the rocks which extensively varies spatially (e.g. Ielsch et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ielsch et al., 2017.

claim: The India Kerala and Iranian Ramsar region have been monitored for their impact on the human mutation rate.
source: While few extremely naturally radioactive sites such as the India Kerala and Iranian Ramsar region have been monitored for their impact on the human mutation rate (Forster et al., 2002; Masoomi et al., 2006) or on plant physiology (Saghirzadeh et al., 2008), the influence of regional variation in baseline natural radioactivity on the evolution of biodiversity is still unknown (Møller and Mousseau, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Forster et al., 2002 and Masoomi et al., 2006.

claim: The influence of regional variation in baseline natural radioactivity on the evolution of biodiversity is still unknown.
source: While few extremely naturally radioactive sites such as the India Kerala and Iranian Ramsar region have been monitored for their impact on the human mutation rate (Forster et al., 2002; Masoomi et al., 2006) or on plant physiology (Saghirzadeh et al., 2008), the influence of regional variation in baseline natural radioactivity on the evolution of biodiversity is still unknown (Møller and Mousseau, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Møller and Mousseau, 2013.

claim: Ionizing radiations damage DNA by breaking the DNA sugar-phosphate backbone.
source: Ionizing radiations damage DNA by breaking the DNA sugar-phosphate backbone (Hoeijmakers, 2001; van Gent et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hoeijmakers, 2001 and van Gent et al., 2001.

claim: Ionizing radiations can trigger the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) directly inside cells through the radiolysis of water.
source: Alternatively, ionizing radiations can trigger the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) directly inside cells through the radiolysis of water (Wallace, 1998; Ward, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wallace, 1998 and Ward, 1988.

claim: ROS are mutagenic.
source: ROS being also mutagenic (Barja, 2002), ionizing radiations are direct and indirect mutagens.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barja, 2002.

claim: Ionizing radiations are direct and indirect mutagens.
source: ROS being also mutagenic (Barja, 2002), ionizing radiations are direct and indirect mutagens.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that ionizing radiation can damage DNA directly and indirectly through ROS.

claim: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are the most deleterious and studied mutations generated by radioactivity.
source: The most deleterious and studied mutations generated by radioactivity are DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about radiation-induced DNA damage.

claim: Two repair systems are able to manage double-strand breaks: homologous recombination (HR) and non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ).
source: Two repair systems are able to manage double-strand breaks: homologous recombination (HR) and non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ).
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: HR uses an homologous sequence to revert the damage, but is only used at specific cell cycles when an undamaged sister chromatid is available.
source: HR uses an homologous sequence to revert the damage, but is only used at specific cell cycles when an undamaged sister chromatid is available (Karran, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Karran, 2000.

claim: NHEJ does not use a template-strand to reconstruct the missing genetic information.
source: As NHEJ does not use a template-strand to reconstruct the missing genetic information, it only restores the continuity of the DNA molecule to the price of frequent deletions and chromosomal exchanges.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about NHEJ mechanism.

claim: NHEJ only restores the continuity of the DNA molecule at the price of frequent deletions and chromosomal exchanges.
source: As NHEJ does not use a template-strand to reconstruct the missing genetic information, it only restores the continuity of the DNA molecule to the price of frequent deletions and chromosomal exchanges.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about NHEJ mechanism.

claim: 50% of the double-strand breaks were misrejoined after a strong irradiation (80 Gy).
source: Rothkamm et al., 2001 showed that 50% of the double-strand breaks were misrejoined after a strong irradiation (80 Gy).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rothkamm et al., 2001.

claim: Exposure to radiation produces chromosomal abnormalities.
source: Numerous studies demonstrate that an exposure to radiation produces chromosomal abnormalities (Dikomey et al., 2000; Loucas et al., 2004; Hande et al., 2005), deletions (Jostes et al., 1994; Huo et al., 2001; Adewoye et al., 2015; Allegrucci et al., 2015), and point mutations (Huo et al., 2001; Winegar et al., 1994; Forster et al., 2002; Barber et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Exposure to radiation produces deletions.
source: Numerous studies demonstrate that an exposure to radiation produces chromosomal abnormalities (Dikomey et al., 2000; Loucas et al., 2004; Hande et al., 2005), deletions (Jostes et al., 1994; Huo et al., 2001; Adewoye et al., 2015; Allegrucci et al., 2015), and point mutations (Huo et al., 2001; Winegar et al., 1994; Forster et al., 2002; Barber et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Exposure to radiation produces point mutations.
source: Numerous studies demonstrate that an exposure to radiation produces chromosomal abnormalities (Dikomey et al., 2000; Loucas et al., 2004; Hande et al., 2005), deletions (Jostes et al., 1994; Huo et al., 2001; Adewoye et al., 2015; Allegrucci et al., 2015), and point mutations (Huo et al., 2001; Winegar et al., 1994; Forster et al., 2002; Barber et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mutational impact of exposure to high doses of radioactivity is well characterized.
source: While the mutational impact of exposure to high doses of radioactivity is well characterized (Dubrova et al., 1996; Ziegler et al., 1993), the exposure to low doses of radioactivity is poorly known.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dubrova et al., 1996 and Ziegler et al., 1993.

claim: The exposure to low doses of radioactivity is poorly known.
source: While the mutational impact of exposure to high doses of radioactivity is well characterized (Dubrova et al., 1996; Ziegler et al., 1993), the exposure to low doses of radioactivity is poorly known.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of scientific knowledge regarding low-dose radiation effects.

claim: Some authors propose that DNA repair and apoptosis may completely counteract the effect of ionizing radiations for doses below 0.1 Gy.
source: Some authors (Tubiana et al., 2006) propose that DNA repair and apoptosis may completely counteract the effect of ionizing radiations for doses below 0.1 Gy, suggesting that low doses have no biological impact.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tubiana et al., 2006.

claim: In vitro experiments on mammalian cells show that repair systems are more efficient to repair DSBs at low dose than at higher dose.
source: Indeed, in vitro experiments on mammalian cells show that repair systems are more efficient to repair DSBs at low dose than at higher dose (Boucher et al., 2004, 0.05 vs 3.5 Gy/min).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Boucher et al., 2004.

claim: Exposure to an even lower dose of ionizing radiation (less than 0.1 cGy/min) increases the number of mutants in mammals.
source: However, exposure to an even lower dose of ionizing radiation (less than 0.1 cGy/min) increases the number of mutants in mammals (Vilenchik and Knudson, 2000; Hooker et al., 2004) suggesting that repair systems are not activated at very low radiation doses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vilenchik and Knudson, 2000 and Hooker et al., 2004.

claim: Repair systems are not activated at very low radiation doses.
source: However, exposure to an even lower dose of ionizing radiation (less than 0.1 cGy/min) increases the number of mutants in mammals (Vilenchik and Knudson, 2000; Hooker et al., 2004) suggesting that repair systems are not activated at very low radiation doses.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that low doses increase mutations.

claim: When repair systems are not activated and DNA damage accumulates, cells tend to die by apoptosis.
source: When repair systems are not activated and DNA damage accumulates, cells tend to die by apoptosis, preventing the transmission of radioactivity-induced mutations to the next cell generation (Rothkamm et al., 2001; Collis et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rothkamm et al., 2001 and Collis et al., 2004.

claim: Unrepaired DSBs are the main cause of radioactivity-induced cell apoptosis during mitosis.
source: Unrepaired DSBs are the main cause of radioactivity-induced cell apoptosis during mitosis (Krueger et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krueger et al., 2007.

claim: Point mutations will not lead to cell death like DSBs.
source: As point mutations will not lead to cell death like DSBs, this type of radioactivity-induced mutations could stay unrepaired and be transmitted to the next generation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the relative severity of different types of DNA damage.

claim: Radioactivity-induced point mutations could stay unrepaired and be transmitted to the next generation.
source: As point mutations will not lead to cell death like DSBs, this type of radioactivity-induced mutations could stay unrepaired and be transmitted to the next generation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the fact that point mutations are less likely to trigger apoptosis.

claim: Exposure to low doses of radioactivity induces an adaptive response where exposed cells are resistant to a following higher dose of radiation.
source: Exposure to low doses of radioactivity also induces an adaptive response: exposed cells are resistant to a following higher dose of radiation (see Rigaud and Moustacchi, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rigaud and Moustacchi, 1996.

claim: An early or chronic exposure to low doses of radiation may strengthen the antioxidant defense and reduce the sensitivity to radioactivity-induced ROS.
source: An early or chronic exposure to low doses of radiation may strengthen the antioxidant defense and reduce the sensitivity to radioactivity-induced ROS.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms of adaptive response.

claim: The adaptive response seems to only protect the nuclear genome while the mitochondrial one may not benefit from it.
source: Moreover, the adaptive response seems to only protect the nuclear genome while the mitochondrial one may not benefit from it (Jarrett and Boulton, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jarrett and Boulton, 2005.

claim: Some studies found an increase in the number of mutations in the offspring of exposed people.
source: Some studies found an increase in the number of mutations in the offspring of exposed people (Dubrova et al., 1996; Forster et al., 2002), while others studies found the opposite (Satoh et al., 1996; Czeizel et al., 1991), leaving open the question of the transmission of mutations generated by low doses of radioactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dubrova et al., 1996 and Forster et al., 2002.

claim: Some studies found no increase in the number of mutations in the offspring of exposed people.
source: Some studies found an increase in the number of mutations in the offspring of exposed people (Dubrova et al., 1996; Forster et al., 2002), while others studies found the opposite (Satoh et al., 1996; Czeizel et al., 1991), leaving open the question of the transmission of mutations generated by low doses of radioactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Satoh et al., 1996 and Czeizel et al., 1991.

claim: Subterranean waterlice are never exposed to UV radiation.
source: Subterranean waterlice are never exposed to UV radiation, live in contrasted bedrock set-ups and have very limited dispersal capacity (Eme et al., 2018), allowing us to make the assumption that different species have persisted in different but nearly constant radioactive habitats for numerous generations.
evidence: This is based on knowledge about subterranean habitats and the biology of waterlice.

claim: Subterranean waterlice live in contrasted bedrock set-ups.
source: Subterranean waterlice are never exposed to UV radiation, live in contrasted bedrock set-ups and have very limited dispersal capacity (Eme et al., 2018), allowing us to make the assumption that different species have persisted in different but nearly constant radioactive habitats for numerous generations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eme et al., 2018.

claim: Subterranean waterlice have very limited dispersal capacity.
source: Subterranean waterlice are never exposed to UV radiation, live in contrasted bedrock set-ups and have very limited dispersal capacity (Eme et al., 2018), allowing us to make the assumption that different species have persisted in different but nearly constant radioactive habitats for numerous generations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eme et al., 2018.

claim: Different waterlouse species have persisted in different but nearly constant radioactive habitats for numerous generations.
source: Subterranean waterlice are never exposed to UV radiation, live in contrasted bedrock set-ups and have very limited dispersal capacity (Eme et al., 2018), allowing us to make the assumption that different species have persisted in different but nearly constant radioactive habitats for numerous generations.
evidence: This is an assumption based on the limited dispersal capacity of waterlice and the stability of bedrock radioactivity.

claim: Fourteen sites with contrasted levels of α radioactivity were selected, each inhabited by closely related groundwater waterlice species.
source: From this large survey (58 sites with waterlice), we selected 14 sites with contrasted levels of α radioactivity which were inhabited by closely related groundwater waterlice species.
evidence: This describes the sampling design of the study.

claim: α radioactivity differed at least by a factor of three between two habitats, each containing a closely related species.
source: We paid special attention that α radioactivity differed at least by a factor of three between two habitats, each containing a closely related species (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for the study sites.

claim: Low level of radioactivity was around 0.357 Bq/g of dry sediment.
source: On average low level of radioactivity was around 0.357 Bq/g of dry sediment and high level around 1.259 Bq/g of dry sediment.
evidence: This is a measurement from the study.

claim: High level of radioactivity was around 1.259 Bq/g of dry sediment.
source: On average low level of radioactivity was around 0.357 Bq/g of dry sediment and high level around 1.259 Bq/g of dry sediment.
evidence: This is a measurement from the study.

claim: Two sites (BRETEMIN and BOREON) show a disruption of the secular equilibrium in the U-238 chain.
source: The analysis of the composition in radionuclides at each site reveals that two sites (BRETEMIN and BOREON) show a disruption of the secular equilibrium in the U-238 chain.
evidence: This is based on radioactivity measurements at the sites.

claim: Nearby industrial activities (e.g. lead mines) have modified the natural radioactivity at BRETEMIN and BOREON sites.
source: This suggests that nearby industrial activities (e.g. lead mines) have modified the natural radioactivity at these two sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the disruption of secular equilibrium.

claim: Industrial activities at BRETEMIN and BOREON are very recent (since 1950).
source: As these industrial activities are very recent (since 1950), their impact on the substitution rate, which is measured on a much longer time scale, is unlikely.
evidence: This is a statement about the timing of industrial activities.

claim: The dS/ra is positively correlated with the α radioactivity in the nuclear genome.
source: The dS/ra is positively correlated with the α radioactivity in the nuclear genome as well as in the mitochondrial genome (Table 1; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in the study.

claim: The dS/ra is positively correlated with the α radioactivity in the mitochondrial genome.
source: The dS/ra is positively correlated with the α radioactivity in the nuclear genome as well as in the mitochondrial genome (Table 1; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in the study.

claim: A linear model predicts a dS/ra increase of 31.8% in the nuclear genome between species living in low and high radioactivity.
source: A linear model predicts a dS/ra increase of 31.8% in the nuclear genome and 56.5% in the mitochondrial genome between species living in low (on average 0.357 Bq/g of dry sediment) and high radioactivity (on average 1.259 Bq/g of dry sediment).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling of the data.

claim: A linear model predicts a dS/ra increase of 56.5% in the mitochondrial genome between species living in low and high radioactivity.
source: A linear model predicts a dS/ra increase of 31.8% in the nuclear genome and 56.5% in the mitochondrial genome between species living in low (on average 0.357 Bq/g of dry sediment) and high radioactivity (on average 1.259 Bq/g of dry sediment).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling of the data.

claim: There are positive correlations between the dS/ra and the received dose of radioactivity.
source: Again, we found positive correlations between the dS/ra and the received dose of radioactivity (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in the study.

claim: The results are robust to the presence of influential cases and to variation in the model of evolution used to perform the test.
source: These results are robust to the presence of influential cases and to variation in the model of evolution used to perform the test (see Methods, pGLS, p. values < 0.05).
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analyses described in the methods.

claim: The nuclear and mitochondrial dS/ra of a species living in a metamorphic formation are on average 34.4% and 61.3% higher, respectively, than those of a species living in a sedimentary formation.
source: The linear model predicts that the nuclear and mitochondrial dS/ra of a species living in a metamorphic formation (>50% of metamorphic and igneous rocks) are on average 34.4% and 61.3% higher, respectively, than those of a species living in a sedimentary formation (<50% of metamorphic or igneous rocks).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling of the data.

claim: The occurrence of G→T mutation increases after exposure to carbon black.
source: The occurrence of this mutation increases after exposure to carbon black (Jacobsen et al., 2011), to tobacco smoke (Hollstein et al., 1991; Hainaut and Pfeifer, 2001), or to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (Nik-Zainal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jacobsen et al., 2011.

claim: The occurrence of G→T mutation increases after exposure to tobacco smoke.
source: The occurrence of this mutation increases after exposure to carbon black (Jacobsen et al., 2011), to tobacco smoke (Hollstein et al., 1991; Hainaut and Pfeifer, 2001), or to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (Nik-Zainal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hollstein et al., 1991 and Hainaut and Pfeifer, 2001.

claim: The occurrence of G→T mutation increases after exposure to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.
source: The occurrence of this mutation increases after exposure to carbon black (Jacobsen et al., 2011), to tobacco smoke (Hollstein et al., 1991; Hainaut and Pfeifer, 2001), or to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (Nik-Zainal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nik-Zainal et al., 2015.

claim: Oxidative stress is the likely source of G→T mutation.
source: Oxidative stress is the likely source of this mutation (Wood et al., 1990; Besaratinia et al., 2004; Jacobsen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wood et al., 1990, Besaratinia et al., 2004, and Jacobsen et al., 2011.

claim: The mutational spectrum modification observed in radioactive environments is suggestive of an increase of the overall oxidative stress in these environments.
source: Thus, the mutational spectrum modification observed in radioactive environments is suggestive of an increase of the overall oxidative stress in these environments.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed increase in G→T mutations, which are associated with oxidative stress.

claim: High artificial doses of ionizing radiation increase oxidative damage.
source: Similarly, high artificial doses of ionizing radiation were found to increase oxidative damage (Einor et al., 2016; Haghdoost et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Einor et al., 2016 and Haghdoost et al., 2006.

claim: Oxidative stress triggers more 8-hydroxyguanine formation in the mitochondrial genome than in the nuclear genome.
source: As oxidative stress triggers more 8-hydroxyguanine formation in the mitochondrial genome than in the nuclear genome (Richter et al., 1988), this could explain the twice as strong effect observed in this study in the mitochondrial compartment.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 1988.

claim: The twice as strong effect observed in the mitochondrial compartment could be explained by oxidative stress triggering more 8-hydroxyguanine formation in the mitochondrial genome.
source: As oxidative stress triggers more 8-hydroxyguanine formation in the mitochondrial genome than in the nuclear genome (Richter et al., 1988), this could explain the twice as strong effect observed in this study in the mitochondrial compartment.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference between nuclear and mitochondrial mutation rates.

claim: The ionisation of molecules in the cells can directly affect the DNA structure by breaking the sugar phosphate backbone.
source: First, the ionisation of molecules in the cells can directly affect the DNA structure by breaking the sugar phosphate backbone or can affect DNA indirectly through the radiolysis of water which decomposes the H2O molecules and create free radicals (Desouky et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Desouky et al., 2015.

claim: The ionisation of molecules in the cells can affect DNA indirectly through the radiolysis of water which decomposes the H2O molecules and create free radicals.
source: First, the ionisation of molecules in the cells can directly affect the DNA structure by breaking the sugar phosphate backbone or can affect DNA indirectly through the radiolysis of water which decomposes the H2O molecules and create free radicals (Desouky et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Desouky et al., 2015.

claim: Free radicals can damage DNA molecules and create mutations.
source: These free radicals can damage DNA molecules and create mutations.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the mutagenic effects of free radicals.

claim: Radioactive decay chains generate heavy metals (lead, polonium, etc) which are toxic for cells and cause oxidative stress.
source: Second, radioactive decay chains also generate heavy metals (lead, polonium, etc) which are toxic for cells and also cause oxidative stress (Quinlan et al., 1988; Pinto et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Quinlan et al., 1988 and Pinto et al., 2003.

claim: In naturae correlative approaches alone cannot discriminate between the toxicity of heavy metals and the direct toxicity of radioactive rays.
source: Due to the physicochemical association between radioactivity and heavy metals, in naturae correlative approaches alone cannot discriminate between the toxicity of heavy metals and the direct toxicity of radioactive rays.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study design.

claim: Metamorphic and igneous rocks are more naturally radioactive than sedimentary rocks.
source: While metamorphic and igneous rocks are more naturally radioactive than sedimentary rocks (Ielsch et al., 2017), they also display characteristic compositional and structural features which may also control species life history traits (Cornu et al., 2013; Eme et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ielsch et al., 2017.

claim: Metamorphic and igneous rocks display characteristic compositional and structural features which may control species life history traits.
source: While metamorphic and igneous rocks are more naturally radioactive than sedimentary rocks (Ielsch et al., 2017), they also display characteristic compositional and structural features which may also control species life history traits (Cornu et al., 2013; Eme et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cornu et al., 2013 and Eme et al., 2015.

claim: Metamorphic and igneous rocks are calcium poor relative to sedimentary rocks.
source: Metamorphic and igneous rocks are calcium poor relative to sedimentary rocks.
evidence: This is based on established geological knowledge.

claim: In isopods, the cuticle is made of calcium carbonate which is acquired by isopods from their environments.
source: In isopods, the cuticle is made of calcium carbonate which is acquired by isopods from their environments (Greenaway, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Greenaway, 1985.

claim: A lower calcium availability may slow down the growth of isopod species.
source: A lower calcium availability may slow down the growth of isopod species.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the effect of calcium availability on growth.

claim: A lower growth rate, if it slows down the generation time, is expected to decrease the mutation rate.
source: However, a lower growth rate, if it slows down the generation time, is expected to decrease the mutation rate, while we observed the opposite.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the relationship between generation time and mutation rate.

claim: Metamorphic and igneous rocks have smaller size and less permeable habitats.
source: Because metamorphic and igneous rocks have smaller size and less permeable habitats, they could support smaller effective isopod population sizes.
evidence: This is based on geological knowledge about rock properties.

claim: The dS is an estimator of the mutation rate that is not directly impacted by the effective population size.
source: The dS is an estimator of the mutation rate that is not directly impacted by the effective population size (Kimura, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kimura, 1983.

claim: Lynch, 2010 proposed that species with small effective population size should evolve higher mutation rate as a result of the accumulation of weakly deleterious mutations in genes involved in repair efficiency and replication fidelity.
source: However, as effective population size modulates the efficacy of natural selection, Lynch, 2010 proposed that species with small effective population size should evolve higher mutation rate as a result of the accumulation of weakly deleterious mutations in genes involved in repair efficiency and replication fidelity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lynch, 2010.

claim: There is no correlation between radioactivity and dN/dS.
source: Here, we found no correlation between radioactivity and dN/dS (pGLS, p.value = 0.3069) suggesting this effect is not at work in this data-set.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The influence of confounding factors that would drive the observed mutational variations is unlikely.
source: Altogether, the influence of confounding factors that would drive the observed mutational variations is unlikely.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of potential confounding factors.

claim: The mitochondrial genome lacks some repair systems.
source: First, the mitochondrial genome lacks some repair systems.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mitochondrial DNA repair.

claim: UV damage accumulates in the mitochondrial genome while they are repaired in the nuclear genome.
source: For example, in a different yet analogous context, UV damage accumulates in the mitochondrial genome while they are repaired in the nuclear genome (Clayton et al., 1974).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clayton et al., 1974.

claim: The nuclear genome is compacted into chromatin.
source: Second, the two genomes have very different organizations: while the nuclear genome is compacted into chromatin, the mitochondrial one is organized into nucleoids (Chen and Butow, 2005).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about genome organization.

claim: The mitochondrial genome is organized into nucleoids.
source: Second, the two genomes have very different organizations: while the nuclear genome is compacted into chromatin, the mitochondrial one is organized into nucleoids (Chen and Butow, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen and Butow, 2005.

claim: The chromatin structure and histone proteins protect the nuclear genome against radiation-induced strand breaks.
source: While the role of the mitochondrial nucleoids is unclear, the chromatin structure and histone proteins protect the nuclear genome against radiation-induced strand breaks (Ljungman, 1991) and oxidative damage (Ljungman and Hanawalt, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ljungman, 1991.

claim: The chromatin structure and histone proteins protect the nuclear genome against oxidative damage.
source: While the role of the mitochondrial nucleoids is unclear, the chromatin structure and histone proteins protect the nuclear genome against radiation-induced strand breaks (Ljungman, 1991) and oxidative damage (Ljungman and Hanawalt, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ljungman and Hanawalt, 1992.

claim: Direct radioactivity damage to the mitochondria may increase the activity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and indirectly increase the production of ROS and DNA damage.
source: Third, direct radioactivity damage to the mitochondria may increase the activity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and indirectly increase the production of ROS and DNA damage (Yamamori et al., 2012; Kam and Banati, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamamori et al., 2012 and Kam and Banati, 2013.

claim: Life history traits are known to be central in controlling the mutation rate in most taxa.
source: While life history traits are known to be central in controlling the mutation rate in most taxa (Nabholz et al., 2008; Bromham et al., 1996; Nikolaev et al., 2007; Smith and Donoghue, 2008), our results suggest that natural variation of radioactivity can have a comparable effect.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Natural variation of radioactivity can have a comparable effect to life history traits on mutation rate.
source: While life history traits are known to be central in controlling the mutation rate in most taxa (Nabholz et al., 2008; Bromham et al., 1996; Nikolaev et al., 2007; Smith and Donoghue, 2008), our results suggest that natural variation of radioactivity can have a comparable effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the magnitude of the observed effect of radioactivity on mutation rate.

claim: A 5-fold increase in generation time in waterlice species results in an increase in mutation rate of similar magnitude to the effect of radioactivity.
